1:
The second word of the psalm is disputed before anything else. Charles Ellicott reports that the old Greek and Latin give be angry rather than tremble, and that the optative mood of our version comes from them, while the Hebrew stands in the ordinary present: the peoples tremble, the earth staggers. John Calvin says the word covers any strong emotion arising either from anger or from fear, and would read this verb and the closing one as futures, so that the nations shall tremble and the earth shall be moved as they did at the giving of the Law, which makes the verse a prediction of the subjection of the heathen world. Augustine of Hippo takes the angry reading and finds its occasion: the peoples who worshipped what they had made were angry when Christ began to be preached after the resurrection. John Wesley restricts the tremblers to the enemies of God and his people, and Adam Clarke to those who oppose the kingdom. Matthew Henry and C.H. Spurgeon both widen it to the subjects: Henry recalling that even Moses feared and quaked at the mountain, though we are not now come to that mount which burned with fire, since then God ruled more by the power of holy fear and now by the power of holy love; Spurgeon asking of the chosen people a solemn yet joyful awe, so that saints quiver with devotion where sinners quiver with terror.

The throne between the cherubim is read as mercy by most. Adam Clarke refers it to the ark, with the symbol of the divine presence on the lid, and infers that sitting there implies graciousness, so that the King terrible to sinners is on a throne of grace to all who fear and obey him; he adds that although the symbol was absent from the second temple the title remained, having been given under the first. Matthew Henry distinguishes the two functions of the same seat, a throne from which law is given and a mercy-seat at which petitions are received, the temple being the royal palace and the innermost room the presence-chamber. C.H. Spurgeon keeps both the grandeur and the nearness, a throne sprinkled with atoning blood and veiled by the covering wings. John Wesley says only that he is present with his people, and Charles Ellicott that the verb is a participle in the original. Adam Clarke reviews the title too: the Hebrew has none, the versions but one assign the psalm to David, one of them refers it to the slaughter of the Midianites, which the mention of Samuel forbids, and an editor he follows would place it at the dedication after the return.

The refrain divides the last part of the entry. Charles Ellicott grants that the received rendering, for it is holy, is grammatically possible, but since the same words recur twice later as a refrain where the masculine is required, he would read Holy is He throughout, which also relieves an awkward construction in the verse following, to be joined closely with this one. Adam Clarke hears in the same words a species of chorus sung very solemnly at the close of each part, and makes the immaculate purity of the divine nature the reason for the worship. Keil and Delitzsch build the whole psalm on it: three parts each closing with that ascription, the third more full-toned than the others, an earthly echo of the threefold cry of the seraphim; and they find the parts so exactly measured, two six-line stanzas in each, that the artistry itself is an argument for the integrity of the text against those who would emend it. John Gill takes the greatness in Zion of the temple and of the church, and Charles Ellicott notes that the rabbins found in the great and terrible name the unspoken four-letter name itself.
4:
The opening clause is hard to construe and each takes a different way out. Keil and Delitzsch reject the majority reading, which carries the clause back to the verb of praise across the refrain that stands between, and call that hazardous; they also refuse to make it an independent clause, since loving cannot be said of a strength but only of its possessor, and they set aside the division of the verse adopted by the old Greek; their own solution makes the loving of judgment an attribute of the king, and the might the fronted object of the verb thou hast established, which elsewhere takes the king’s throne for its object. John Wesley reaches the same sense by a shorter road, calling the king’s strength a known Hebraism for the strong or powerful king. John Gill and C.H. Spurgeon read the words as they stand, of a might that delights in right: Gill noting that so potent a prince is yet no tyrannical one, and Spurgeon that the power never exerts itself tyrannically. Adam Clarke takes the verse of the human king who wrote it, as one who was God’s deputy, whose strength was God himself and whose pattern for equity and judgment was God’s own.

C.H. Spurgeon presses the establishment of equity hardest. It is not a court of equity merely but equity itself that is set up, and not for an occasion but as a standing institution, stable as the throne; not even for the sake of mercy will God remove or injure the equity of his moral government; most kingdoms have an establishment of some kind and it is generally inequitable, but here the establishment is equity itself, and the executive is as righteous as the legislative. He adds a complaint about his own time, that men are continually arraigning the government of God and setting up to judge whether he does right, where saintly men of the olden time humbly submitted instead.

The footstool is identified by elimination. Adam Clarke lists the things elsewhere so called — the earth, the city, the temple, the tabernacle and the ark — and settles on the ark, noting that worshippers turned their faces toward it as the place of the symbol of the divine presence. Charles Ellicott renders the command as prostrate yourselves, reviews the same range, and concludes that since the throne above the cherubim has just been named we must think here either of the ground on which the ark stood or of the ark itself. John Wesley agrees that it means before the ark, and then does something none of the others do: he refers the refrain that follows to the footstool rather than to God, taking it to mean that the place is consecrated as a pledge of the divine presence. Adam Clarke keeps the refrain as the burden chanted by the chorus, and John Gill turns the whole verse into a list of ways to exalt the King, in heart and in speech, in private and in public.
6:
Whether the three names belong to the past or the present is the question that divides the entry. Charles Ellicott reads them as present: a Moses and an Aaron among his friends, and a Samuel among those that call upon his name, the poet enhancing the sacred character of the services of his own day by likening its ministers to the heroes of old, much as we might mark a period of scientific achievement by saying that we have a Newton or a Bacon among us. A merely historical reference, he argues, would be both abrupt and inaccurate, since Moses was not a priest and God did not speak to Samuel in the cloudy pillar. Keil and Delitzsch grant that the expression certainly sounds as if it referred to the present, and report that one expositor therefore explained the three as heavenly intercessors after the manner of a vision in the later Jewish books; they reject it, both because it presupposes an active manifestation of life in those who have fallen happily asleep, which is at variance with what the psalms early and late suppose about the other world, and because it founders on the next verse, where God speaks from the pillar. Everyone else reads plain history: the poet appealing, as they put it, to three heroes of the olden time and the events recorded of them.

How Moses can be counted among the priests is answered five ways. John Gill observes that he officiated before Aaron was called, and that it was he who consecrated Aaron and installed him by sacrifice. Matthew Henry adds that for this reason the Jews call him the priest of the priests. Adam Clarke and John Wesley both say simply that he executed the office before the priesthood was instituted. C.H. Spurgeon goes further: though not ordained to the typical priesthood he was a true priest, as Melchizedek had been before him, for God has ever had a priesthood beside and above that of the law. Charles Ellicott turns the same difficulty into evidence, using it to show that the reference cannot be historical at all. C.H. Spurgeon also distinguishes what each of the three saw of the divine holiness, the flaming fire of the law, the fire that devoured the sin offering, and the judgment on the house of Eli, and makes all three stand in the gap as intercessors.

The cloudy pillar and the forgiveness close the psalm. John Gill notes that the speaking from the pillar ceased when the people reached the land, and wonders whether God may have spoken to Samuel out of a cloud as well, since it thundered when he called. Adam Clarke reads the pillar as the means by which all their marchings and encampments were directed, and turns the next clause into an exhortation: they kept his testimonies, so do the same. John Wesley restricts the speaking to some of them. On the vengeance taken of their inventions Adam Clarke says God spared the people but showed his displeasure, chastising without consuming, and John Wesley distinguishes the intercessors who were answered from the people who were forgiven. Charles Ellicott refers the clause not to the persons named at all but to the people at large, and draws the inference the poet leaves unstated, that as the prayers of the ancient saints often procured forgiveness without averting punishment, so the present community must expect retribution when sinful, in spite of the mediation of the better part of the nation; the signs of comparison are missing, he explains, because the Hebrew style did not favour similes. John Gill and Adam Clarke close where the psalm closes, with the chorus repeated for the third time and the worship directed to the holy hill.
